title: The one-letter meter
hook: ajai alai abhai abai: unconquerable, indestructible, fearless, unchanging (Jaap, ek achhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, khal khanddan, breaking the cruel, and your line, break cruelty, adorn earth. Today, Jaap's most compressed meter, where the words almost all start the same way.

Say ah. Just the sound, mouth open, nothing else. It's the sound at the doctor's office, the sound of relief when you sit down after a long day, the sound of surprise. In Gurmukhi it has its own letter, airha, near the very start of the alphabet. Now put that sound at the front of almost every word in a stanza, and build the whole meter on it. Jaap Sahib has one.
screen: `SAY AH.` → `A SOUND WITH ITS OWN LETTER.` → `A STANZA BUILT ON IT.`

segments.voice: The meter is called ek achhari. Ek is one, achhar is a letter: the one-letter meter. Sikh teachers explain the name in more than one way, but you can hear the plainest reason straight away: almost every word in these stanzas begins with the same letter, the a that means without. The first line: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Four words, four doors closing on four old fears. Ajai: jai is victory, being conquered, so ajai is unconquerable. Nobody defeats the One. Alai: lai is dissolving, being destroyed, so alai is indestructible. Nothing wipes the One away. Abhai: bhai is fear, so abhai is fearless. Abai: bai is age, wearing down, so abai is ageless, unchanging. Listen to what's underneath. Defeat, destruction, fear, decay: call them four shadows over a human life, losing, being wiped out, being afraid, getting old. And each is answered with a single short a. After the long names, the Persian titles and the doubled words, the praise here gets very small and very fast. Some reciters fly through these lines so quickly they sound like rain on a roof, as if the hymn has run out of room for anything but the essentials. And Jaap keeps coming back to one of these four in particular. Tomorrow, the one in the middle: abhai.
screen: `EK ACHHARI: THE ONE-LETTER METER.` · `AJAI: UNCONQUERABLE. ALAI: INDESTRUCTIBLE.` · `ABHAI: FEARLESS. ABAI: UNCHANGING.` · `FOUR SHADOWS, FOUR SHORT ANSWERS.` · then, large: `AJAI, ALAI, ABHAI, ABAI.`

segments.voice: Say the four words slowly, with a breath after each: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Then say them a little faster, the way they're recited, and feel the rhythm. Stop, and sit with the open sound of a, the one at the front of every word.
Ek achhari. The one-letter meter, where nearly every word begins with a: ajai, alai, abhai, abai — unconquerable, indestructible, fearless, unchanging.
Your line: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Four shadows, and four short answers to them. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the ek achhari stanzas near the end of Jaap Sahib very quickly, and many know the line ajai, alai, abhai, abai by heart.

chat.says: Why do so many words in that part of Jaap start with the same sound?
options: It's the ek achhari: each opens with a, without, so ajai is unconquerable, abhai fearless.
It just makes the lines easy to memorize; the a doesn't change the meaning.
The a stands for Akal, so each word is only another way of saying Timeless.
chat.meaning: In the one-letter meter, nearly every word opens with a, meaning without: unconquerable, indestructible, fearless, unchanging.
